KORE US Reit completes spec suite development at Washington office complex
article:
KORE US Reit (KORE) has completed a speculative suite (spec suite) development at The Plaza Buildings, an office complex in Washington, US.

It is the Reit's fourth full-floor spec suite development and its second at The Plaza Buildings, KORE said in an Oct 13 release. The Singapore-listed Reit (formerly Keppel Pacific Oak US Reit) is managed by KORE US Reit Management, which is jointly owned by Keppel and KORE Pacific Advisors.

Under KORE's spec suite strategy, asset enhancement initiatives are carried out at vacant offices under its portfolio, turning them into move-in-ready spaces designed to attract tenants and lower long-term capital expenditure associated with tenant turnover.

The latest spec suite development at The Plaza Buildings comprises an entire floor that is now dubbed The Post. Spanning 15,400 sq ft, it features six studio suites designed for small and mid-sized occupiers, alongside an amenity hub with collaborative workspaces, breakout areas, and other shared facilities.

According to KORE, half of The Post’s six suites were leased prior to the development’s completion, with “strong leasing interest” for the remaining units.

“We are encouraged by the pace of leasing and rental performance achieved to date, as we continue to deliver workplace solutions that align with occupier demand,” added David Snyder, CEO of the manager.

KORE's previous full-floor spec suite developments include The Greenhouse at The Plaza Buildings and Ventuno at 1800 West Loop South, an office tower in Houston. The Reit also undertook the repositioning of 1150 Iron Point, an office building in Sacramento, California, following the vacancy of a long-term tenant.

All three developments became fully leased following delivery, the manager said.

The Reit currently has over 35,000 sq ft of additional spec suites under development. This includes more projects at The Plaza Buildings, as well as ongoing developments at Great Hills Plaza and Westech 360, both located in Northwest Austin, Texas.

title: Beauty World Plaza makes fresh collective sale bid at $165 mil
article:
Beauty World Plaza , a 999-year leasehold mixed-use development on Upper Bukit Timah Road , has been launched for collective sale via a public tender exercise, with a guide price of $165 million.

The guide price translates to $2,231 psf of gross floor area, said marketing agent ETC (a member of Realion Group) in an Oct 13 release.

The fresh en bloc bid follows past tender launches for Beauty World Plaza in June 2019 and November 2018. The development was similarly priced at $165 million in both exercises.

Beauty World Plaza is an eight-storey development comprising commercial shops on Levels 1 to 3 and residential apartments on Levels 4 to 8. There is also an open terrace on Level 4.

The development occupies a corner plot along Upper Bukit Timah Road and Bukit Timah Link measuring 24,817 sq ft. The land is zoned for commercial and residential use, with a gross plot ratio of 3.0. It is adjacent to Beauty World MRT Station on the Downtown Line.

The site offers buyers “flexibility to explore different strategies”, said Swee Shou Fern, ETC’s head of investment advisory. “Beyond a conventional redevelopment play, the buyer can also consider asset enhancement for the existing development.”

According to ETC, outline planning permission for serviced apartments has been granted for the site's residential component. The site could yield 108 keys, based on a minimum unit size of 35 sq m (377 sq ft).

“The in-principle planning approval opens up the potential to convert the upper floors to serviced apartments or co-living residences and curate the commercial podium for retail, F&B, lifestyle amenities, enrichment centres or coworking space…subject to authorities’ approval,” Swee commented.

Beauty World Plaza is close to several upcoming developments that are reshaping the Beauty World precinct. These include an integrated transport hub linking Beauty World MRT Station with a new bus interchange, along with The Reserve Residences (an integrated development comprising 732 apartments and retail mall Bukit V) and the 158-unit condo 8@BT .

“Beauty World Plaza is extremely well-placed to benefit from this transformation, given its immediate access to the MRT station and established residential, education and lifestyle catchment,” said Swee.

The development is close to several educational institutions, with Pei Hwa Presbyterian Primary School located within a 1km radius, while Bukit Timah Primary School and Methodist Girsl’ School (Primary) are within a 2km radius.

Within the wider vicinity, tertiary institutions such as the Singapore Institute of Management, Singapore University of Social Sciences and Ngee Ann Polytechnic are a short drive away, along with international schools such as Singapore Korean International School and Chatsworth International School.

The tender will close at 3pm on Nov 19.

title: Vietnam leads Apac branded residences market by number of units, ranks third globally
article:
Vietnam has topped the Asia Pacific (Apac) branded residences market by number of units, with 16,135 residences across 68 completed and pipeline developments.

This makes it the third largest in the world, behind the United Arab Emirates (84,972 units) and the US (71,592 units), according to Global Branded Residences, a UK-based advisory firm that specialises in the market.

The data, compiled in The Brand Standard, the firm’s inaugural annual report, shows that Vietnam has the highest number of branded residential units in Apac despite having fewer developments compared to Thailand, which ranked second. The runner-up has 14,141 branded residences across 73 completed and pipeline projects.

India ranked third for both, with 13,908 residences across 61 developments.

Riyan Itani, founder of Global Branded Residences, notes that while the sector is “usually” measured by the number of developments, looking at the number of units offers further insight. “Counting the residences inside those developments tells you how much product is actually coming to market and how significant the buyer demand actually is.”

In any case, the Apac branded residences market continues to grow, backed by a sizeable pipeline. According to the report, the number of pipeline schemes has surged 36% over the past 12 months, going from 147 projects to 200.

Combined with its 198 completed developments, the region has a total of 398 schemes. It accounts for 20% of global branded residences stock, after North America (452 projects or 23%) and the Middle East and North Africa (Mena) (426 projects or 22%).

Vietnam, Thailand drive growth

Vietnam is currently the biggest contributor to Apac’s pipeline, with 49 projects located across cities such as Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City as well as coastal destinations including Da Nang, Phu Quoc, Hoi An and Ha Long. These include Mercure Residences Ha Long, a 2,259-unit scheme that is the single-largest branded residential development in Apac.

The pipeline is the sixth-largest for a country globally, following the UAE, the US, Mexico, Brazil and Saudi Arabia. Vietnam has completed 19 projects to date.

Thailand is the region’s next-biggest driver, with 37 pipeline developments and 36 completed ones. With 73 projects overall, Thailand is the fifth-biggest market among standalone countries by number of schemes. It is also the third largest for completed stock.

A key market within the country is Phuket, with Global Branded Residences estimating 19 pipeline developments on the Thai island, on top of 13 completed projects. In terms of standalone cities, Phuket is the fifth-largest market in the world by overall developments, behind Dubai, Miami, São Paulo and New York.

All but one of Phuket’s 32 total schemes are in resort locations. This makes it the “largest resort branded residences market in the world”, competing in scale with major capital and gateway cities. “That tells us branded residences are increasingly following international buyers into destinations where lifestyle and leisure are fundamental to the purchasing decision,” adds Itani.

Broader market

The report also highlights that Apac offers a broader spectrum of offerings that reach a wider base in contrast to the North America, Mena and Europe markets. “It has a much wider spread of price points, a strong regional brand ecosystem and an increasingly resort-led pipeline,” says Itani.

Luxury projects account for 61% of Apac’s schemes, compared to 76% for North America. In addition, the region accounts for 54%, 35% and 33% of the midscale, upper-midscale and upscale schemes globally, despite making up less than a quarter of overall stock.

Apac branded residences are also able to command a slightly higher premium versus equivalent non-branded residences. According to the report, Apac schemes have an average price premium of 47%, compared to the global average of 44%.

The premium may reflect the dominance of hotel brands in the region, along with the significance of its resort destinations.

Hotel brands account for 78% of Apac’s overall branded residence schemes, and 82% of pipeline projects. Meanwhile, some 93% of Apac’s resort schemes carry a hotel brand.

Nonetheless, Apac remains the only region worldwide that is not led by Marriott or Accor. The two hospitality giants dominate branded residences elsewhere, making up more than a quarter of overall developments globally.

However, in Apac, Banyan Group leads with around 50 projects, surpassing Accor at 44 and Marriott at 34.

title: Frasers Property appoints ESR's Jai Mirpuri as CEO of industrial and logistics business
article:
Frasers Property has named Jai Mirpuri as the new CEO of Frasers Property Industrial, with effect from Jan 11, 2027. Based in Singapore, Mirpuri will report directly to Frasers Property group CEO Panote Sirivadhanabhakdi.

He will replace Reini Otter, who will be stepping down on Dec 17. Otter is leaving to join ESR Group , where he will be CEO of its Australia and New Zealand business. He spent 28 years at Frasers Property, including seven years as CEO of Frasers Property Industrial.

Mirpuri will helm Frasers Property's industrial and logistics operations in Australia and Europe, which includes overseeing the manager of Singapore-listed Frasers Logistics & Commercial Trust.

He joins the group from ESR, where he is currently the CEO of ESR Fund Managers and head of Southeast Asia. Before that, he was also the founder and co-CEO of ESR India.

He has been with ESR for over 18 years, having joined in 2008.

“Jai brings deep expertise in the industrial and logistics sector, and a strong track record of building teams and managing platforms,” said Sirivadhanabhakdi in an Oct 13 release. “These credentials, combined with his extensive leadership and customer experience across markets, make him well-placed to drive Frasers Property Industrial’s next phase of growth.”

title: Balestier Regency relaunched for collective sale at unchanged price of $255 mil
article:
Balestier Regency , a freehold 10-storey apartment at 4 Jalan Ampas, has been relaunched for collective sale by public tender with a guide price of $255 million.

The price is unchanged from when the 72-unit development last launched for tender in May.

“Given the limited availability of sizeable freehold redevelopment sites in the city-fringe market, we believe Balestier Regency remains a relevant acquisition opportunity for developers taking a medium- to long-term view of the market,” commented Low Choon Sin, managing partner of SRI Capital Market in an Oct 13 release. SRI is handling the sale of the site.

The price reflects a land rate of approximately $1,473 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr), including a land betterment charge (LBC) of about $381,181 (based on September 2026 rates).

If the LBC and bonus gross floor area (GFA) for balconies are factored in, the land rate works out to $1,437 psf ppr.

Completed in 1990, Balestier Regency occupies a 61,931 sq ft residential site with a gross plot ratio of 2.8. This translates to a maximum GFA of approximately 173,407 sq ft.

As the development enjoys a high baseline of 2.793, only a nominal LBC is payable, according to SRI. The site can potentially be redeveloped into a new project with up to 161 apartments.

The tender will close at 3pm on Nov 12.

title: Binjai Park shop with 999-year leasehold tenure on the market for $4.4 mil
article:
A strata-titled commercial unit in Binjai Park has been launched for sale through an expression of interest (EOI) exercise at a guide price of $4.4 million.

The ground-floor unit has a 999-year leasehold tenure and spans a strata area of around 1,388 sq ft, which means the price works out to $3,170 psf. The unit is part of a three-storey walk-up shophouse that includes residential units on the upper floors.

The walk-up sits along a row of similar shophouses in the Binjai Park residential enclave in Bukit Timah. It is within walking distance of the King Albert Park MRT Station on the Downtown Line.

The unit up for sale is currently tenanted, according to Huttons Asia, which is handling the sale.

Yeo Khee Liang, associate senior marketing director at the firm, says that commercial units in the Binjai Park estate are rare. “Only around 16 such units are available within the area.”

As a result, he anticipates the property to appeal to a diverse range of buyers. “We expect strong interest from investors and family offices, as well as owner-occupiers such as boutique operators and wellness or education businesses looking for a foothold in this enclave.”

Lee Sze Teck, Huttons’ senior director of data analytics, notes that the shophouse segment “continues to attract wealth, underpinned by favourable interest rates, constrained supply and foreign ownership regulations elsewhere in the property market”.

title: Late tycoon Chng Gim Huat's Lornie Road bungalow back on market at $83 mil
article:
The sprawling freehold bungalow at 8 Lornie Road, formerly the home of the late property tycoon Chng Gim Huat, is back on the market with a guide price of $83 million, or $1,605 psf.

The 51,700 sq ft estate in prime District 11 is being offered for sale by public tender, with Knight Frank Singapore appointed as the exclusive marketing agent.

The property was first launched for sale by private treaty in May 2025 at $82 million, or $1,586 psf. The Chng family subsequently withdrew it from the market. The latest asking price is up $1 million, or 1.2%.

The relaunch follows the family's June sale of the 272-room Orchid Hotel at 1 Tras Link in Tanjong Pagar for about $273 million. Developed by Chng's CGH Group, the hotel opened in 2011.

The buyer of Orchid Hotel was reportedly a joint venture majority-controlled by an entity linked to Leow Ban Leong, one of the two owners of Singapore-based construction and property group Master Contract Services. North America-based Westmont Hospitality Group holds a minority stake in the joint venture. Knight Frank also brokered the hotel sale.

Family home dating back to 1937

The pre-war bungalow at 8 Lornie Road dates back to 1937 and is believed to have been purchased by Chng in the 1970s from the late Kwek Hong Png, founder of Hong Leong Group and father of City Developments Ltd (CDL) executive chairman Kwek Leng Beng.

Chng, who died in August 2024 at 90, lived in the house with his wife and seven children — five sons and two daughters.

Over the decades, the house was expanded to accommodate the growing family. In the 1990s, the family added two bedrooms to the second floor and built an office suite for the family's investment holding company, Chng Gim Huat Holdings, on the ground floor.

The estate also has an expansive garden with mature fruit trees, including durian, mango, avocado, longan, pomelo and starfruit.

In a May 2025 interview with EdgeProp Singapore, Chng's son Alex recalled how the family would gather in his father's office after dinner to discuss business.

Chng also acquired an adjoining bungalow plot in 1987 and redeveloped it into two pairs of semi-detached houses -- one for four of his four sons.

Redevelopment potential

According to Knight Frank, the 8 Lornie Road site has about 58m of road frontage and offers redevelopment potential.

When the property was first marketed in 2025, Knight Frank indicated that the site could be subdivided into six detached houses or 16 semi-detached houses, subject to approval by the relevant authorities.

Alternatively, the site could be retained as a single private estate for a multigenerational family.

"Beyond its immediate redevelopment potential, 8 Lornie Road offers the opportunity to secure a substantial freehold estate in a market where opportunities of this nature are increasingly difficult to replicate," says Dayna Ang, senior manager of capital markets at Knight Frank Singapore.

Alternatively, the site could be retained as a single private estate for a multigenerational family.

Ang considers the guide price of $1,605 psf on land "an attractive entry point" for buyers with a long-term investment horizon.

Melvin Chay, interim head of capital markets at Knight Frank Singapore, says the firm continues to see interest from developers and private investors in well-located freehold residential assets.

"While developers are focused on development feasibility and end-buyer demand, private buyers tend to place greater emphasis on location, privacy and long-term ownership," he says.

The tender for 8 Lornie Road will close on Nov 12 at 3pm.

title: Your $10,000 is shrinking. Smart Investors Fight Back.
article:
When people realize their savings are shrinking because daily expenses are climbing, the immediate response is often panic or pinching pennies.
A $10,000 cash buffer in the bank might feel comfortable today, but at a modest 2% inflation rate over ten years, that same $10,000 will only buy $8,000 worth of goods.
If inflation creeps up to 4%, its purchasing power plummets to around $6,600.
Cash in the bank will not protect you from rising prices, and bonds generally won’t either.
To
beat inflation
, you need assets that grow over time.
Since not everyone can drop a million dollars on a private condominium overnight, investing in the stock market remains one of the most accessible and effective tools available.
The Secret Ingredient: Pricing Power
When inflation strikes, smart investors don’t just cut back on expenses; they look for companies that can pass cost increases directly onto consumers.
That ability is called pricing power, and it is one of the most valuable traits a business can possess.
Think about consumer staples.
When prices rise, people don’t stop taking showers or washing their clothes. Personal care companies can adjust pack sizes or incrementally increase prices without losing loyal customers.
The same goes for local
daily staples
.
If a bakery increases the price of a curry puff by 10 cents and consumers keep buying it, that business has pricing power.
You can spot pricing power in your everyday life:
Consumer Goods:
Look at the brands you buy automatically, like the mobile phone from your favourite brands or daily household essentials.
Commercial Real Estate:
Observe packed shopping malls on weekends. Busy foot traffic benefits the
real estate investment trusts (REITs)
that own those properties.
Essential Services:
Pay attention to businesses that remain busy regardless of economic headlines, from fast-food chains to streaming platforms.
Whenever you buy a product, turn the item over or look around the shop floor.
Ask yourself:
Who makes this? Is their revenue growing? Are their profits rising? Do they pay a reliable dividend?
Balancing Your Investment Recipe
To build a resilient portfolio targeting long-term returns of 8% to 10%, you need the right mix of growth and income.
If you only buy stocks with massive 8% or 9% dividend yields, you will collect handsome payout cheques, but those businesses often lack room for capital growth.
Conversely, a 2% dividend yield might seem small at first, but reinvesting those payouts back into more shares creates a
compounding snowball
.
The extra shares pay you more dividends, which you then reinvest to buy even more shares.
Managing a portfolio is like cooking: you have to balance the seasoning.
You need income-generating stocks to provide steady cash flow, paired with growth-oriented businesses that expand your overall capital.
Get Smart: Conviction Beats Market Volatility
Inflation is an invisible tax on idle cash, but you can turn it to your advantage by owning cash-generative businesses with strong pricing power.
When you invest in companies that raise their prices and grow their payouts over time, you build an income stream that keeps you ahead of rising costs.

title: The AI Boom Is Being Built on Debt: Should Investors Be Worried?
article:
Big Tech companies
such as
Meta Platforms
(NASDAQ: META) and
Alphabet
(NASDAQ: GOOGL) were previously known for their cash-rich, fortress balance sheets.
Their financial firepower to fuel the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution was nearly undisputed.
But now, debt is increasingly being used instead to finance data centres, specialised silicon, and the massive grids to power them.
The narrative has shifted from smart AI agents powering the future economy to a grim future of mounting financial debt that could drag down global growth.
Should investors be alarmed?
What Happened to Their Fortress Balance Sheets?
Historically, Big Tech operated as asset-light enterprises.
Their capital expenditure (capex) as a percentage of revenue was reportedly low, in the single digits (about 4%).
Today, the capex at the hyperscalers (the largest cloud-computing providers) amounts to more than half of their revenues.
Collectively, the AI spending by the four hyperscalers – Alphabet,
Amazon
(NASDAQ: AMZN),
Microsoft
(NASDAQ: MSFT), and Meta – is projected to surge 84% in 2026 to US$760 billion.
Crucially, global debt funding towards the AI infrastructural buildout is expected to double, reaching nearly US$570 billion in 2026, and to increase further as the hyperscalers’ capex is tipped to surpass US$1 trillion in 2027.

Corporate bond sales surged 11.8% to US$2.46 trillion in 2025, driven by US hyperscaler-linked issuances.
But the real financial shift lies in off-balance-sheet financing structures.
To preserve their credit ratings, the tech giants are turning to special purpose vehicles (SPVs), private credit, and graphics processing unit (GPU)-backed securitisations.
Consider Meta’s private capital deal with
Blue Owl Capital
(NYSE: OWL), which resulted in the two entities forming an SPV that issued over US$27 billion in private debt backed by Meta’s lease commitment and financial guarantees.
Under this deal, private-credit funds hold 80% of the SPV’s equity while Meta holds the remaining 20% in the Louisiana project.
Importantly, this minority stake allows Meta to keep the associated liabilities off its balance sheet.
Meta is not alone.
Collectively, Big Tech’s off-balance-sheet commitments have reportedly reached US$3.1 trillion, roughly four times greater than their expected capex of US$760 billion in 2026.
Related articles:
Meta Platforms vs OCBC: Which Stock Creates More Value for Shareholders?
If You Invested US$10,000 in Meta at Its IPO, Here’s How Much You’d Have Today
Silicon Obsolescence and Mounting Costs
With such massive leverage, the structural risks are real.
While massive capital to build AI-related hardware is spent upfront at unprecedented speed, the software running on it is monetised much more slowly.
To make matters worse, hardware generally depreciates much faster than software.
Critics have observed that the hyperscalers have artificially stretched the depreciation timelines of their GPUs to aggressively lower expenses and boost their profit margins.
On top of that, the recurring operating expenses of US$2.0 million to US$2.8 million per megawatt per year add pressure to the hyperscalers’ profitability.
A Systemic Bubble?
Rising debt to fund fast-depreciating hardware, without meaningful software revenue to offset it, does not paint a reassuring picture for investors.
Moreover, the true leverage might be understated due to the off-balance-sheet arrangements that obscure the full extent of financial obligations.
Crucially, the risks are interconnected among stakeholders.
Hyperscalers,
neoclouds
(young cloud-computing companies that focus on providing GPUs to customers), private-credit funds, sovereign investors, and even pension funds are linked through contracts and securitised debt, meaning any stress incurred in one of the nodes could send ripples across the whole ecosystem.
A Secular Boom?
Using debt to fund infrastructure is not uncommon, especially for the AI revolution, which is frequently touted as a once-in-a-lifetime industrial revolution.
Despite asset depreciation risks, AI data centres may stay useful for longer than expected, as older computing capacity can be repurposed for less demanding tasks.
What about the risk of a demand shortfall?
Arguably, this is unlikely, given AI’s wide total addressable market that spans across software development, healthcare, finance, manufacturing, research and public services.
What about leveraged players defaulting? That is possible for weaker players.
Therefore, investors should focus on the best-capitalised hyperscalers, which run some of the most profitable, cash-generating business models with healthy margins and strong balance sheets.
They are more likely to survive a shakeout and emerge even stronger.
Get Smart: How Investors Can Navigate the AI Debt Era
The
AI boom
isn’t inherently doomed by debt, but the era of premium valuation multiples is ending as investors demand more visibility for their investments.
Furthermore, given the enormous scale of AI infrastructure, funding it through debt could be considered rational, if done responsibly.
Still, the real risks will surface if spending accelerates with no end in sight while free cash flow dries up and visible returns stall.
For investors, the important question is therefore not “Is AI being built on debt?” but “Can the companies borrowing and investing today generate enough future cash flow to justify that debt?”
Balance-sheet transparency, favourable debt coverage, and monetisation potential should define the winners in the
next phase
of the boom.
Not all AI “winners” will survive this cycle.

The aim is to make

So, has trading volume risen?
What Changed with SGX’s Board Lot Size Reduction?
Before 5 October, all 11 stocks traded in lots of 100 shares, the standard since January 2015, when SGX cut it from 1,000.
Under the new rules, stocks priced between S$10 and S$100 can trade in lots of 10 shares, and those above S$100 in single shares.
So far, only the
first 11 qualifying stocks
have switched.
Together, the 11 stocks made up roughly 35% of SGX trading activity in the first half of 2026.
Only the minimum order size changes, so the share prices, dividends per share and valuations stay untouched.
A stock that moves to a smaller lot keeps it even if its price later falls, and the Singapore Exchange (SGX) will review more stocks every quarter from January 2027, using July to December closing prices.
For stocks priced above S$10, buying in lots of 10 instead of 100 cuts the cost of entry by 90%.
SGX expects the change to lower barriers to participation and improve affordability for retail investors.
More participation could, in turn, support liquidity.
Did Trading Volume Actually Increase?
The banks make a poor test case.
On 7 October 2026, OCBC fell 5.9% after Citi downgraded it to sell, and DBS and UOB also closed lower.
Moves like that lift volumes on their own, so the analysis looks at five eligible names less affected by the bank sell-off: SGX, Keppel, Jardine Cycle & Carriage, Haw Par Corporation and Venture Corporation.
We compare two periods: the 20 trading days from 7 September to 2 October, before the change, and the five sessions from 5 to 9 October, after it.
We look at two measures: average daily volume (ADV), which is the number of shares traded each day, and average daily value, which is the number of shares traded multiplied by the closing price.

However, we don’t see this effect flow to SGX and Venture Corporation, both priced higher than Keppel.
Four of the five stocks saw a higher average daily value.
That said, we caution that there are nuances to the data: too few trading sessions have passed and short-term trading volumes may be driven by market sentiment, individual company announcements or general trading conditions.
Why Smaller Board Lots Could Encourage More Trading
The most obvious draw is the lower upfront cost.
Previously, one lot of DBS shares cost roughly S$7,300; now, you can buy shares of the bank with just about S$730.
That also makes it easier to spread money around.
About S$900 now buys 10 shares each of SGX, Keppel, Jardine Cycle & Carriage, Haw Par Corporation and Venture Corporation.
Previously, such a basket would have cost roughly 10 times as much.
Regular investing gets easier too.
Before, an investor who set aside S$500 a month would take about 15 months to buy one board lot of DBS shares; now, it takes just two months.
The Catch: Brokerage Fees Still Matter
Many brokers charge a minimum commission per trade, and a small order feels it most.
A hypothetical S$27 minimum fee on a S$730 purchase (10 DBS shares) works out to 3.7% of the amount, compared with just 0.37% on S$7,300.
Over a round trip, the share price must climb about 7.4% just to break even for the former and roughly 0.74% for the latter.
What you pay depends on the type of
brokerage account
.
Traditional brokers have usually charged a percentage commission with a minimum fee of roughly S$8 to S$27, though some have started reducing minimums on small trades since the change.
Lower-cost trading platforms charge far less, typically a small percentage with a minimum of a few dollars, or none at all.
A lower entry price only helps if commissions stay small relative to the amount invested.
Anyone who buys 10 shares at a time also pays that commission on every purchase.
What Should Investors Watch Next?
It’s too early to tell whether the pickup in trading will last.
The real test is whether volumes stay above their pre-change pace moving forward.
The next few months of trading data should reveal plenty.
Total volume is only part of the picture.
Large institutional orders can swamp it, so the share of trades below 100 shares, the number of trades and the median trade size are better gauges of small-investor participation.
A lower entry price also changes nothing about what the underlying company earns; share prices will still follow earnings and dividends.
Get Smart: Accessibility Is Only the First Step
Smaller lots put the market’s priciest stocks within reach of small investors.
The early trading data is encouraging but far from conclusive.
Four of the five stocks recorded higher average daily volume than before the change.
Jardine Cycle & Carriage posted the biggest jump.
At about S$25, it is the highest-priced of the five, but company news may also have played a part: it is selling its Cycle & Carriage motor businesses, is changing its name and has proposed a special dividend.
If a high share price alone drove trading, SGX and Venture, both priced above Keppel, should have gained more than Keppel did, but they didn’t.
Transaction costs matter, too, so check your broker’s fee schedule and avoid trading just because it’s cheap to start.
The real test is whether liquidity and participation hold up over several months, not one busy week.

title: Legacy carmakers seen losing mass market to Chinese rivals
article:
(Oct 13): Legacy carmakers won’t likely be able to match Chinese rivals on price and may already have missed first-mover advantage on electric and software-developed vehicles, according to a report by Mobility Global Inc’s automotive analysts.

The paper, which the research firm released on Tuesday, projects established automakers will retain the upper hand over newer, China-based peers in areas such as premium brands, safety-based engineering and fleet sales. But Chinese carmakers have an edge in mass-market vehicles from sheer scale, faster development and lower costs.

“The competition is just going to become more intense,” Calum MacRae, an executive director at Mobility Global and one of the report’s authors, said in an interview, noting global demand for passenger vehicles is sluggish. “That competitive pressure is coming within a total industry volume that’s probably not going to grow significantly.”

The report, entitled New Order: China, the West and the battle for automotive advantage, said that while China’s rise as a globally competitive auto power echoes that of Japan and South Korea, Chinese carmakers benefit from the widespread impact of software, which is reshaping business models, and easier access to capital as part of China’s effort to foster a home-grown auto industry.

See also: Nobel Peace Prize bets for Navalny widow surge on Polymarket

“This shock is different because China’s advantages are much harder to replicate. What is being imported now is either a software-driven experience with rapid feature updates or a cost advantage that is reinforced by preferential financial and supplier-backed working capital,” it said.

The global auto industry is struggling to come to terms with an influx of Chinese-made vehicles. That has led some governments to restrict or effectively ban vehicle imports from China, which Mobility Global views as a precursor to a boom in local production by Chinese automakers in overseas markets — first by investing in existing plants and then building new ones.

China-based manufacturers are already seeking joint ventures with some established European automakers as a way to absorb excess production capacity. That allows them to access existing logistics networks and workforces, while drawing on their own supply chains for core components. As their market share grows, Chinese brands will opt to build new plants on their own.

See also: Germany and France push trade weapon to deny access to China

Construction of BYD’s electric vehicle plant in Szeged, southern Hungary in August.

Mobility Global, which spun off from S&P Global Inc in July, projects that output from those newly built, or so-called greenfield, factories in Europe will exceed that from older, or brownfield, facilities as soon as 2030 — when localised production of Chinese brands nears an estimated 1.1 million vehicles.

Brownfields offer a “low risk, low friction option” initially, Mobility Global’s MacRae said, adding that “once you’ve established that you can get a market position, it’s natural that you start localizing production and investing in your own facilities.”

BYD Co, China’s largest carmaker, is looking to skip existing JVs altogether and move straight to building its own factories. Stella Li, who head’s the company’s overseas business, told Bloomberg on Monday that it plans to become a major manufacturer in Europe by the end of the decade, and aims to hire as many as 40,000 workers there. In addition to building a plant in Hungary, it’s eyeing new factories in France and Spain.

MacRae said that it’s difficult to predict whether Chinese automakers will penetrate the US market, where imports from China are largely blocked. But he noted brands like Great Wall Motor Co make a wide range of vehicles such as pickup trucks that might one day appeal to cost-sensitive American buyers.

title: Data centre operator AirTrunk is said to delay US$1.5 billion IPO
article:
Data centre operator AirTrunk is delaying a planned initial public offering of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until next year as higher interest rates and market volatility temper investor demand, according to people familiar with the matter.

The Blackstone Inc-backed company had been planning to start formally gauging investor interest for the US$1.5 billion REIT IPO at the start of October, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.

A planned IPO in Australia by another data centre company, Firmus Grid, collapsed last week. The Nvidia Corp-backed firm failed to bring in enough demand at the valuation it sought, reflecting growing investor caution about artificial intelligence infrastructure deals that hinge on future earnings.

To sweeten its deal for investors, AirTrunk had considered offering a roughly 6% yield for its REIT, up from a previously envisaged 5.5%, the people said. However, September’s interest rate rise in the US and the prospect of further increases mean investors are still cautious, they said.

REITs are rate-sensitive and therefore come under pressure when borrowing costs are high. The data centre subsidiary of Philippine telecommunications firm PLDT Inc said last week it would defer its REIT IPO to next year given rising interest rates. Singapore’s main REIT Index has tumbled 12% since late July.

AirTrunk’s deliberations over details such as the size and timing of the potential IPO are ongoing, the people said.

See also: Bursa-listed IOI Properties Group in talks for secondary listing on SGX

Dow Jones Newswires reported earlier that AirTrunk was delaying plans for the Singapore listing because of market volatility and uncertainty over US rates.

Representatives for AirTrunk didn’t respond to requests for comment. Blackstone declined to comment.

AirTrunk, which was founded in Sydney in 2015, operates data centres in Australia, Hong Kong, India, Japan, Malaysia and Singapore, according to its website. In 2024, Blackstone and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board acquired the company for A$24 billion (US$16.7 billion) in what was Blackstone’s biggest-ever investment in the Asia Pacific region.

title: US small-business optimism falls on dimmer economic outlook
article:
(Oct 13): US small-business optimism fell to a three-month low in September as economic expectations dimmed and a smaller share of firms indicated it was a good time to expand.

The National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB) index slipped 0.8 of a point to 97.9, according to data out on Tuesday. Six of the 10 components that make up the gauge declined, while three rose and one held steady. A measure of uncertainty crept higher as well.

The net share of owners who expect business conditions to improve declined four percentage points to a four-month low of 6%.

Persistent price pressures continue to weigh on small businesses as military conflict in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war keep energy costs high. Last month, 20% of businesses said inflation was their single biggest problem, nearly three times the historical average of 7%, according to NFIB.

A net 31% plan to raise their own prices in the next three months, up from 28% in August and July.

With inflation stubborn and borrowing costs elevated, small businesses are more cautious about expanding. Capital spending plans dropped to a three-month low.

See also: US consumer sentiment falls to five-month low in October

“Small-business owners are proceeding with caution as they interpret how rising costs, interest rates, and the difficulty in finding qualified employees are impacting their business,” NFIB chief economist Bill Dunkelberg said in a statement.

Some 26% of firms, up three percentage points from August, said labour quality or availability was their single most important problem.

title: Billionaire Kotak says India should let rupee find its own level
article:
(Oct 13): Billionaire banker Uday Kotak said India should allow its currency to find its own footing, arguing that uncertainty over policymakers’ intentions can keep markets guessing as global capital flows shift.

“My personal view is we should let the rupee find its own level and, over time, the true strength of the economy will play out,” Kotak said at Bloomberg’s New Economy Forum in New Delhi.

A prolonged disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has pushed up crude oil prices and unsettled global markets, putting the rupee under pressure against the US dollar.

The Reserve Bank of India has stepped up efforts to contain the volatility in the local currency, which is down close to 6% against the dollar this year. The central bank has publicly said it intervenes to curb volatility in the foreign exchange market and does not target any particular level of the rupee.

Kotak said that if markets do not know of a level the policy maker is trying to justify, “the markets will be guessing.”

Kotak, India’s richest banker, has a net worth of US$15.8 billion, the majority of which is derived from a 26% stake in Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd, India’s fourth-largest private bank by assets.

See also: India’s rupee gains most in Asia as RBI widens currency curbs

The shift in global capital flows should also serve as a signal for India to strengthen its economic competitiveness, efficiency and domestic capabilities, Kotak said.

“And at the same time, India has to consider this as an important signal that we need to do a lot more to be competitive, efficient, self-reliant and stronger in our research and innovation,” Kotak added.

title: Hong Kong investigates IPO rigging, suspends Baicha stock
article:
(Oct 13): Hong Kong’s securities watchdog is investigating a suspected case of rigging an initial public offering (IPO) to create a false impression of demand.

The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) directed the stock exchange to suspend Sichuan Baicha Baidao Industrial Co’s trading from 9am on Oct 13 in Hong Kong. The regulator said it has “serious concerns that Baicha’s IPO may have been rigged”, according to a statement sent Tuesday after the market closed. The company’s market value is HK$5.9 billion (US$752 million or $960 million).

Baicha raised about US$330 million ($422 million) in April 2024 in what was at the time Hong Kong’s biggest first-time share sale of the year. Its shares plunged 27% on their first day and never traded above the offer price. China International Capital Corp was the sole sponsor of the IPO. The retail tranche was 0.5 times subscribed, while institutional investors bid for 1.1 times the shares initially made available.

Hong Kong is in the midst of a bumper year for IPO proceeds, driven by a series of listings by Chinese companies along the artificial intelligence supply chain. As dealmaking ramped up, with hundreds of listings in the pipeline, authorities have sounded the alarm on deal quality. They’ve also begun to tighten scrutiny of bankers’ resources and document quality.

Separately, the SFC issued restriction notices to 31 brokers, prohibiting them from dealing with or processing assets relating to two syndicates on three IPOs. The first syndicate is linked to the listing of Baicha, as well as that of Cloudbreak Pharma Inc The regulator restricted dealing in assets held in client accounts of up to HK$4.4 billion — the largest such notice in SFC history — among six brokers.

The watchdog also restricted 29 brokers to deal assets of up to HK$285 million in client accounts related to the IPO of Tianju Dihe (Suzhou) Technology Co Ltd.

See also: Segantii insider trading trial ends with verdict due February

“We believe that the actions taken to date have significantly disrupted two suspected syndicates which may have been involved in IPO-rigging cases,” SFC’s executive director of enforcement Michael Duignan said in the statement.

The brokers who received the restriction notices aren’t the subjects of the SFC’s investigations. The restriction notices do not affect the brokers or their other clients, the watchdog said in the statement.

The SFC said its investigations are continuing and it won’t make any further comments while they are underway.

title: Space investment to top US$100 bil in 2026 after SpaceX IPO
article:
(Oct 13): Investment in the space economy is on track to exceed US$100 billion for the first time ever in a given year in 2026, fuelled by SpaceX’s blockbuster initial public offering, defence spending and space infrastructure.

The prediction stems from a new analysis of third quarter spending from Space Capital, an investment firm. On top of quantifying the sheer amount of investment, the report also notes that more space companies are reaching unicorn status than ever before.

“We all thought that 2021 was this crazy hot market,” Chad Anderson, CEO of Space Capital, said, referring to the blank-check deal frenzy of the time. “It looks like a blip compared to what’s happening now.”

To explain the surge, all roads lead back to SpaceX.

Anderson said SpaceX’s record-setting IPO this summer may have led investors to revalue other space companies, viewing them as more essential than they might have before.

However, SpaceX is having an impact beyond its IPO. The company’s intention to sunset its Falcon 9 workhorse in the years ahead creates the threat of a rocket shortage that is fuelling investments in SpaceX alternatives.

See also: Addvalue’s shareholders give green light for proposed spin-off, proposed dilution

Launch startup Stoke Space Technologies, Inc., for instance, recently announced that it had raised US$1 billion to fuel development of a larger variant of its reusable Nova rocket. SpaceX’s largest rival, Blue Origin LLC, also raised at least US$10 billion in its first external fundraising in the company’s 26-year history.

“This is the best thing to happen to the launch industry in a decade,” Anderson said. “This is how the second, third and fourth position companies come about. The scarcity is driving the market to adopt additional solutions.”

Space Capital’s report also notes that the investment is being bolstered by high demand for space assets from the US government’s defence department as well as from sovereign nations looking for their own satellite networks and other space infrastructure to fuel economic growth.

See also: Addvalue partners Viasat to deliver IDRS to US government fleets

However, the free-flowing money does carry risk for companies. Firms are raising money at incredibly high valuations that do not often add up, Anderson says, especially if they have built their business models around an uncertain variable. For instance, one big risk for the space industry now is being too reliant on SpaceX.

“There are some companies getting funded today that, for example, require SpaceX’s Starship to build their business and launch their satellites, and that’s a big risk,” Anderson said. “I don’t know when they’re going to make that capability available.”

title: EuroSports Global ends JV discussion with Helios Power Systems
