title: Asian stocks to fall after US chipmaker sellof
article:
(Oct 13) : Asian stocks were set to decline as a selloff in chipmakers weighed on sentiment ahead of a pivotal earnings season and US inflation data that could shape the Federal Reserve’s next move.

Equity-index futures for Japan, Hong Kong and South Korea pointed lower, while those for Australia edged higher. US stock contracts were little changed after a gauge of chipmakers fell 2.7% and the Nasdaq 100 lost 0.7%. Treasury futures fluctuated ahead of the resumption of cash trading following a US holiday. A Bloomberg gauge of dollar strength climbed to its highest since mid-May 2025.

Micron Technology Inc. fell 3.9% and US-listed shares of SK Hynix Inc. dropped 4% after Chinese rival CXMT said it made progress on a memory-chip design capable of storing more data. Sandisk Corp. slid 6%, among the S&P 500’s biggest decliners.

Enthusiasm for artificial intelligence eased as investors weighed the outlook for capital spending against rising borrowing costs. Wall Street’s equity bull entered its fifth year, with the S&P 500 up nearly 120% from its 2022 low, putting the onus on earnings growth to justify elevated valuations.

“Growth has been powerful enough to keep valuations in check and allow investors to look past higher yields, interest rates and inflation,” said Bret Kenwell at eToro. “Another strong quarter could reinforce the bull narrative intact into year-end, while a disappointment could catalyze a broader pullback.”

US oil edged lower in early trading after Brent advanced 1.8% Monday as Ukraine cast doubt on an “energy ceasefire” touted by US President Donald Trump and Saudi Arabia faced fresh Houthi attacks following the deadliest strikes since the start of the Iran war.

See also: Oil holds advance as expanding Middle East war threatens supply

“We now expect Brent crude to average above US$100 a barrel through the second quarter of next year following attacks on Red Sea export infrastructure and a more persistent geopolitical risk premium,” Stephen Hare, lead economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a note. “Prices decline thereafter as supply normalizes, but the return towards long-run equilibrium is now slower than previously expected.

The earnings season in the US gets underway Tuesday, with Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase & Co., Citigroup Inc. and Wells Fargo & Co. due to report. Bank of America Corp. and Morgan Stanley follow Wednesday. S&P 500 companies are estimated to post a 25% increase in third-quarter profits from a year earlier, according to data compiled by Bloomberg Intelligence.

Investors will also be focusing on Wednesday’s consumer price index, likely the most important economic report the Fed will see before its October meeting.

See also: Bank stocks mired in correction into earnings as yields rise

Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack said smaller, more frequent policy adjustments can help keep inflation expectations anchored, though she stopped short of backing another rate increase this month.

“This week’s CPI report is likely to be the most important release of data the Fed will see before its October meeting,” Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy and research at Glenmede, wrote. “Barring a stronger than expected inflation reading, the Fed is likely to take a patient approach to its next rate hike.”

title: Oil holds advance as expanding Middle East war threatens supply
article:
(Oct 13) : Oil held a gain as a widening conflict in the Middle East threatened to hamper a recovery in supply from the region, while there were also doubts over US President Donald Trump’s claims of an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine.

West Texas Intermediate traded near US$93 a barrel after rising 2.1% in the previous session, while Brent settled near US$107 on Monday. A barrage of drone and missile attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia’s main airport has intensified pressure on Washington to step up its efforts in the conflict in Yemen.

Meanwhile, Ukraine will continue attacks against Russia as Moscow keeps targeting its energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Trump said there had been were violations of his “energy ceasefire” but urged his Ukrainian counterpart and Russian President Vladimir Putin to come together and end the war.

Brent remains more than 70% higher this year as the US war on Iran roils energy markets. The attacks on Saudi Arabia came shortly after Riyadh-led forces in Yemen launched a campaign to retake Houthi-held territory, while strikes on tankers in the critical Strait of Hormuz have escalated — leading a growing number of vessels to turn away from a port in the United Arab Emirates that has been key in helping Persian Gulf oil exports recover to near prewar levels.

“Its been a dizzying few days of headlines,” said Scott Shelton, an energy specialist at TP ICAP Group, pointing to issues including Trump’s claims of an “energy ceasefire” as well as the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. “We are off to a messy start this week.”

title: Bank stocks mired in correction into earnings as yields rise
article:
(Oct 13) : Big US bank stocks are teetering in correction territory as the group kicks off earnings Tuesday, heightening the focus on executives’ outlook for the American consumer with long-term borrowing costs the highest in decades.

Wall Street’s largest banks are expected to unveil a quarterly stock-trading haul of nearly US$19 billion, according to analyst estimates compiled by Bloomberg. Meanwhile, lending is seen increasing year-over-year and credit quality is likely to hold steady, analysts expect.

Even so, the benchmark KBW Bank Index has dropped around 12% since a mid-August peak, exceeding the 10% threshold for a technical correction. The slump has coincided with a surge in Treasury yields and the Federal Reserve’s first interest-rate hike in three years. The bank gauge is coming off its worst quarter since early 2023, when a prior episode of rising yields helped trigger a regional bank crisis that hit shares.

Banks, which need to balance how much they pay out for deposits with what they earn on loans, have been stung by the bond volatility, and they’re also under pressure as rates on credit-card, auto and home loans are climbing, says Matt Miskin at Manulife John Hancock Investments.

Lenders can benefit as “higher yields can lead to better revenues, but they can also lead to a tipping point where consumers just can’t pay these kinds of loans,” said Miskin, a strategist.

Reports from the banking giants start rolling in before the market opens on Tuesday, with announcements from Citigroup Inc., Goldman Sachs Group Inc., JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Wells Fargo & Co. On Wednesday, Bank of America Corp. and Morgan Stanley report.

See also: US stocks waver on slowest trading day in 2026

Last month, early reporter Jefferies Financial Group Inc. said its investment bank and equity-trading desk had a record quarter, though other metrics were mixed.

Options traders were leaning bullish on JPMorgan, the largest US bank, before the results, trading at the end of last week showed. Demand for upside calls that pay out on a 10% move outweighed the appetite for insurance against a 10% drop. Plus, there were more calls outstanding than puts, a potentially bullish signal.

So far, the economy is proving resilient in the face of higher borrowing costs and elevated energy prices, which have fanned inflation concerns. Investors in bank shares have other worries, such as risks posed by artificial-intelligence agents and the potential fallout from the November midterm elections, with polls showing Republicans losing ground amid voter anger over the economy and the war in Iran.

See also: Oil rises on Mideast attacks, dollar edges high

Republicans tend to favor lighter oversight of the financial sector, leading JPMorgan analysts to predict that a surprise sweep by the party could favor lenders such as Bank of America, Citigroup and Wells Fargo.

Wells Fargo’s Mike Mayo is among the analysts with a more bullish take on bank shares. He said last month that the elections can “put a dent in de-regulation but should not derail it.” He was also optimistic the AI “scare trade” would reverse when banks release results as “trust at banks is a moat for deposits.”

And at Morgan Stanley, analyst Manan Gosalia called the selloff lately “an attractive entry point,” and recommended investors use it to position for a stronger 2027.

The analyst pointed to AI-related investing and an overall sturdy economy as supporting bank shares. As for rising interest rates, while that does raise banks’ cost of funding, “at the same time revenue should also move higher,” Gosalia said.

As for the coming days, CIBC Capital Markets strategist Christopher Harvey anticipates executives will express more caution about consumer health and the economy than they did a few months ago.

Nonetheless, the sector may be headed for a “relief rally,” he wrote in a Monday note. Banks have typically bounced after earnings when they’ve been lagging going into the announcements, he said.

And if that does happen, “we would use the pop as an opportunity to reduce exposure” given the macro headwinds the firms are facing. He prefers communication services and utilities sectors over financial stocks.

title: LVMH sales at key unit fall as China woes hurt Louis Vuitton
article:
(Oct 12): LVMH’s biggest division posted a slump in sales last quarter as its key Louis Vuitton brand suffered from a boycott in China.

Organic revenue at the fashion and leather goods unit slid 5% in the third quarter, LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE said in a statement on Monday. Analysts were expecting a drop of 1.57%.

The division was “affected in the third quarter by the slowdown in demand in China,” LVMH said.

Louis Vuitton sales suffered in July and August in China after the brand won a trademark dispute against Molly Tea, a local tea maker, Bloomberg reported last month. The victory drew a backlash from Chinese consumers there who deemed it unfair of the world’s largest luxury group to take the much smaller company to court.

LVMH shares have fallen by more than 40% this year, putting them on track for the worst annual performance since the global financial crisis in 2008. While much of the industry is feeling the effects of the downturn in demand, LVMH’s stock is the worst performer this year among major luxury groups, followed by rival Hermes International SCA.

Hopes for a rebound in the wider luxury industry this year have been undermined by sluggish Chinese demand, the prolonged conflict in the Middle East and weaker consumer confidence.
